conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You’re here because of nausea and vomiting again, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been vomiting all day. I tried the Zofran I have at home, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your blood sugars—how have they been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been in the 150s to 200s. I took my Lantus last night at 10, like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. No signs of diabetic ketoacidosis, which is reassuring. Did you eat anything this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried some toast and soda, but I threw it all up. Then my back pain got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, diarrhea, or other symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no belly pain or anything like that. Just the nausea, vomiting, and now my back is really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. In the ER, you got some IV Zofran, ketorolac, and Dilaudid. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea is calmer, but my back still aches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing that. Your labs look stable—no infection, kidneys are okay, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried about my sugars or kidneys again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Since you have type 1 diabetes, we want to avoid both high and low sugars. You had one mild low this morning, but you treated it with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, around 6 AM. I had some juice and it came back up. But I ate a cracker after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good job catching that. We’ll keep your insulin the same as before—no changes to your Lantus or Novolog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I don’t want to go too low again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now, about the nausea—since Zofran ODT isn’t helping at home, we’re suggesting you try Ativan next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ativan? Like for anxiety? But I’m not anxious when I’m nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with nausea too, especially in people with diabetes. It works on the brain’s nausea center. And since you already take lorazepam, it’s safe to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So instead of Zofran, take Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1 mg. We’re updating your prescription so you can try it next time symptoms start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll give it a shot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve been doing well—no vomiting since this morning, and you sipped some broth without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel much better. Still a little queasy, but not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to advance your diet to a regular diabetic meal tomorrow. If you keep this up, you could go home tomorrow afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on gabapentin—200 mg three times a day. It’s for nerve-related pain and might help more than tizanidine did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t keep taking tizanidine—it didn’t help. But I liked the lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But insurance requires a trial of gabapentin first. If this doesn’t work, we can apply for the patches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I have to try this first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And you can increase the dose slowly—by 200 mg each week, up to 400 mg three times a day, if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So start at 200, then go up if it’s not helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But don’t go over 1200 mg a day unless we say so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I can still use the menthol cream and acetaminophen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both are fine. Use them as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did great overnight—no vomiting, ate breakfast without issues, and your sugars are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. Keep taking the gabapentin daily, even if your back feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it doesn’t help, I can call about the lidocaine patches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Also, try Ativan next time nausea starts. And keep following up with your new care team, especially the Chronic Pain Service.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if you really need us.
